# Agentic & A2A Use Cases

## Kagenti Platform

Kagenti is a Kubernetes operator for AI agent lifecycle management, licensed
under Apache 2.0, with six architectural layers spanning deployment, identity,
networking, observability, governance, and development [15][16].

## AuthBridge Identity Injection

AuthBridge injects three sidecars into agent pods: spiffe-helper (for SVID
management), kagenti-client-registration (for Keycloak integration), and an
Envoy proxy (for mTLS enforcement). The agent container itself remains
unmodified [15][18].

SPIFFE identities are auto-injected as X.509 SVIDs, scoped to the namespace and
service account of the agent workload [18].

## SPIFFE vs API Keys for Agents

The case against API keys for agent identity is stark: 70% of leaked secrets
remain active for 2 years. SPIFFE-issued SVIDs are auto-rotated and
cryptographically bound to the attested workload, eliminating the credential
leakage risk [18].

## Agent Card Signing

Agent Cards are signed using JWS with an x5c header that embeds the full
certificate chain, making them self-verifying without requiring out-of-band key
distribution. Kagenti supports both audit and strict enforcement modes [3].

## A2A Protocol

The A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol uses Agent Cards as the discovery mechanism.
Communication follows JSON-RPC 2.0 conventions, with cards discoverable at a
well-known URI [21].

## MCP Authentication

MCP (Model Context Protocol) mandates OAuth 2.1 for authentication and supports
mTLS. However, over 2,000 public MCP servers currently operate without any
authentication [32].

## Kagenti ADK

The Kagenti Agent Development Kit wraps agents with operational infrastructure
including identity, networking, and observability. It supports RFC 8693 token
exchange (SPIFFE SVIDs exchanged for JWT tokens) and integrates with 15+ LLM
providers [17].

## Istio Ambient Mesh Integration

Istio Ambient mode deploys a ztunnel per-node proxy for L4 mTLS enforcement.
Unauthorized requests receive an HTTP 000 response (connection reset) [18].

## Vault for Agent Identity

HashiCorp Vault 1.21 introduced native SPIFFE authentication for AI agents.
Vault 2.0 adds a SPIFFE secrets engine capable of issuing SVIDs directly [13].

## Gaps and Limitations

1. The A2A protocol is in its early stages, with limited production deployments
   and evolving specifications [33].
2. While 91% of organizations are adopting AI agents, only 10% have governance
   strategies in place [33].
3. Agent identity frameworks remain immature, with most solutions addressing
   class-level identity (per service account) rather than per-instance identity
   [31][26].
4. 51% of external agent actions use hard-coded credentials, indicating that the
   industry has not yet adopted workload identity practices for AI agents [34].
